analysis.one_liner: Forces the EPA to tighten air-pollution limits on cancer-causing ethylene oxide emissions within nine months.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee at the end of the 115th Congress with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Ethylene oxide is a gas used to sterilize medical equipment. The EPA's own 2016 science found it is far more dangerous than previously believed — its cancer risk estimate rose 30-fold — and the agency has since loosened, not tightened, some of its rules. This bill would have required the EPA, within nine months, to review and rewrite the emissions standards for ethylene oxide sources, including sterilization chamber vents that the EPA stopped requiring companies to control in 2001. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or send their kids to school near ethylene oxide sterilization plants and other facilities that emit the gas. The EPA's air-toxics assessment found ethylene oxide is the biggest driver of cancer risk in 93 of the 100 census tracts with the highest air-pollution cancer risk nationwide, and in 58 of those tracts the risk exceeds 100 cases per million — the level EPA treats as a public health threat. Tighter standards on chamber vents would cut those emissions at the source.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near ethylene oxide sterilization plants

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to complete a review and issue a final rule revising ethylene oxide emissions standards within nine months of enactment, rather than waiting for the agency's optional eight-year review cycle.

Specifically requires new standards under Clean Air Act section 112(d)(2) to control emissions from sterilization chamber exhaust vents — a requirement the EPA eliminated in 2001 and which, per the bill's findings, is a significant contributor to the elevated cancer risk in the EPA's National Air Toxics Assessment.

Restores the eight-year revision cycle the Clean Air Act already mandates: the standards for commercial sterilization facilities were last updated in 2006 and for hospital sterilizers in 2007, both before the 2016 finding that the gas's cancer risk is 30 times higher than the 1985 estimate.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that run ethylene oxide sterilization facilities — contract sterilizers and hospital sterilizer operations — would bear the cost of installing or upgrading emission controls on chamber vents and other sources. Those costs could partly pass through to hospitals and device makers that depend on sterilization services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ethylene oxide sterilization facilities and hospitals

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on a small number of sterilization facilities; if those costs are significant, some could pass through to hospitals and medical-device makers that rely on ethylene oxide to sterilize surgical instruments and single-use equipment, and an abrupt or poorly designed rule could disrupt that supply.

The nine-month deadline for a final rule is unusually fast for a major air-toxics rule, which critics of rushed rulemaking could argue leaves less room for the technical analysis and comment that a facility-specific standard normally gets.
The bill does not provide funding or compliance relief, so the entire burden of the tighter controls falls on the regulated facilities rather than being shared or phased in by legislation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit is targeted but potentially large: the EPA's own data show ethylene oxide drives the top cancer risk in dozens of communities, and the chamber vents at the center of this bill have been uncontrolled since 2001. The cost is real but narrow — a handful of facilities installing emissions controls for a known human carcinogen, a cost that is the normal price of operating under air-toxics law. On balance the bill's benefits to nearby residents outweigh its costs, though a faster-than-normal rulemaking timeline is a fair criticism.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup, and expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Daniel Lipinski introduced the bill on November 20, 2018, late in the second session of the 115th Congress.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on November 20, 2018, and that was the final action in its history.
The 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019, so the bill died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ethylene oxide sterilization facilities are better off: they face no new requirement to control chamber vent emissions, which the EPA eliminated in 2001. Residents near those facilities continue to live with the elevated cancer risk the EPA's own assessment identified.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sterilization plants; nearby residents keep the risk

for.name: Rep. Daniel Lipinski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the EPA to revise ethylene oxide emissions standards within nine months, including controls on sterilization chamber vents.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Colleagues in the House
against.what_they_did: No member signed on as a cosponsor during the bill's six-week life.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew enough support to reveal a partisan pattern: a lone Democrat sponsored it, no Republicans or other Democrats cosponsored, and no vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Medical sterilization facilities (contract sterilizers and hospital sterilizer operations)
industries.note: The bill would force these facilities to install controls on sterilization chamber vents and meet tighter emissions standards for a known human carcinogen. Their cost of compliance is directly the public health benefit for people living nearby, since EPA data show the gas drives the top cancer risk in most of the country's most polluted census tracts.

industries.industry: Ethylene oxide producers and users in manufacturing
industries.note: The bill targets emissions standards for 'sources of ethylene oxides' broadly, so chemical plants and other industrial emitters could face revised standards too. The narrower chamber-vent provision, however, is aimed at sterilization facilities.
